beats.care: If someone in your family needs cancer treatment, the same medicine could cost far less. Families pay about three quarters of cancer costs themselves.
beats.what: The government capped what distributors and chemists can keep on many cancer medicines. Their share can be at most 30 percent of the MRP.
beats.why: Officials found the markup between the company's price and the MRP averaged about 170 percent, and sometimes reached 700 percent.

cards.body: Many cancer medicines aren't price-controlled, so distributors and shops could add huge markups. The new rule caps their cut at 30% of the MRP, for branded and generic, Indian and imported drugs. An expert panel picks the final list; its report is due 14 Oct.
That's the government's estimate; real savings depend on which drugs make the final list.
cards.caption: Estimated yearly savings for patients

cards.body: It's the gap between what the drug company charges and the MRP you pay. Distributors, wholesalers and chemists share it. The company's own selling price doesn't change under this rule; only the middle chain's share gets squeezed. Makers must also keep production at current levels so supply doesn't dry up.
cards.title: what's a trade margin?

cards.body: This has worked before. In 2019, a similar 30% cap on 42 cancer drugs cut prices of some brands by up to 91%.
